blocks.text: Give an object its collaborators from outside, usually through the constructor, instead of letting it create or look them up.

A class declares what it needs as constructor parameters typed by **interface**. A single **composition root**, usually `main` or a container, creates the objects and connects them. The class stays ignorant of concrete implementations and lifetimes, so tests pass fakes and configuration swaps real ones.

items: **Setter or field injection:** optional, mutable, easy to forget.

blocks.text: Dependency injection is a technique and needs no framework. A container only automates the composition root.

walkthrough.note: The consumer depends on a small interface that it defines in its own vocabulary, not on an SMTP or HTTP class.
Collaborators arrive through the constructor and are null-checked. Time itself is injected as a `Clock`, so overdue logic is deterministic.
The composition root builds the graph and picks implementations: a fixed clock keeps the demo deterministic, where production would pass `Clock.systemUTC()`.
A test wires the same class differently: a later clock and a capturing mailer. Nothing inside `InvoiceReminder` changed.

blocks.text: Testing a payment service against a fake gateway.

`PaymentService` needs a gateway, an idempotency store and a clock. In production a container injects an HTTP gateway client; in tests the constructor receives a scripted fake that fails twice, then succeeds. Retry logic, timeouts and expiry are tested in milliseconds without network or sleeping.

lines: var gateway = new ScriptedGateway(FAIL, FAIL, OK);
var svc = new PaymentService(gateway, store, clock);

blocks.text: Payoff: failure paths that are hard to provoke in integration environments become ordinary unit tests.

lists.title: Use when
items: A class has collaborators that tests must replace: time, network, storage.
You want dependencies visible in the constructor signature.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A value is a trivial pure helper: a plain `static` call or `new` is clearer.
Wiring is a one-line obvious choice and nothing is ever replaced.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Constructors with eight or more parameters usually signal a class doing too much.
Injecting the container itself, which turns DI into a [Service Locator](kata:service-locator).
Circular dependencies hidden by setter injection.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: An interface and a factory for every class with exactly one implementation.
Wiring spread across annotations, XML and code, so no one can see the graph.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Constructor injection with records or `final` fields makes required collaborators immutable.

rows.difference: With a locator the class asks a global registry for its dependencies, hiding them. With DI they are pushed in and visible in the constructor.
The Dependency Inversion Principle says depend on abstractions; DI is the common mechanism that supplies the concrete one.
A factory creates collaborators on demand inside the class. Injection hands them in ready, and the class never builds them.
Injecting a strategy is DI, but DI also supplies collaborators that are not interchangeable algorithms, like a clock or a repository.
Containers manage lifetime, so a singleton scope replaces hand-written global `getInstance()` with an injected shared instance.

entries.name: ApplicationContext and constructor injection
entries.detail: The container resolves constructor parameters by type; `@Autowired` is optional on a single constructor.

entries.name: jakarta.inject.Inject (CDI)
entries.detail: Standard annotation for injection points, resolved by a CDI container.

entries.name: Guice Injector and Dagger
entries.detail: Guice wires at runtime from modules; Dagger generates the wiring at compile time.

entries.name: java.time.Clock
entries.detail: Abstract class designed as an injectable time source, with `Clock.fixed` for tests.

options.why: Collaborators come in through the constructor as abstractions; one outer place chooses the implementations.
Nothing is looked up from a registry; the dependencies are explicit constructor parameters.
`Clock` and `Sink` are collaborators of different kinds, not interchangeable algorithms for one decision.
The class doesn't create anything, and no factory family appears.

exercises.scenario: `ReportJob` opens its own JDBC connection and builds an HTTP client in the constructor. Tests hit real services, and the staging environment needs a different mail server than production.

options.why: Pass the connection source and clients in as interfaces; tests and environments differ only in the composition root.
A registry still hides the needs and fails at runtime if something is missing.
A global instance would make tests share state and still wouldn't let staging differ.
A subclass overriding a creation method would couple environment choice to inheritance.

exercises.prompt: Explain dependency injection: who creates dependencies, where, and how it differs from a service locator.

modelAnswer.text: A class declares its collaborators as constructor parameters and never creates or finds them itself. One composition root builds the graph and chooses implementations. Unlike a service locator, the dependencies are explicit in the type signature, missing ones fail at compile or startup, and tests simply pass fakes.

keyPoints: Collaborators are passed in, usually via constructor
One composition root wires the graph
Dependencies are visible in the signature
Locator hides them and fails at runtime
